title: Annual traffic counts on PTH 12 and 52: used to lobby for intersections, never to measure through traffic or trucks
summary: Every year since 1997 the city has paid for peak-hour intersection counts on PTH 12 and PTH 52 (MMM, then WSP). Council accepted each report (2016-2026) and usually forwarded it to the province with requests for signals or intersection work: Industrial Rd (2017), Loewen Blvd (2018-2020), Giesbrecht St (2022 onward). Members called the counts the evidence for lobbying on provincial highways. The studies count turning movements at about 20 intersections for a few weekday hours; council never asked for an origin-destination survey or a truck count. Members did read through-traffic patterns into them: Damian Penner noted more traffic 'going through' from growing Mitchell (2022).
status_detail: Reports accepted each year (2018-01-02 consensus; R20-034, R21-046, R22-038, R23-056, R24-054, R25-060, R26-037). Requested intersection work followed (Industrial Rd signals, Loewen rebuild 2025, Giesbrecht signals 2026). No through-traffic or truck data was requested; the 2026 resolution, unlike earlier ones, did not say to forward the study to the province.
figures: Counts since 1997 (Zwaagstra, 2026-02-17, 0:21:48); 18 intersections in 2017 with daily volumes on PTH 12 and 52 and three daily peaks at PTH 12/52: 7:30-9:30 a.m., noon, 3:30-5 p.m. (minutes 2018-01-02, item 6); growth 1-3% a year over 10 years (minutes 2018-01-02; transcript 2017-01-17 0:03:28).
reasons: provincial-highway: highways are provincial; the city can only advocate, with data (Michael Zwaagstra)
seconder: Siemens (R20-034); Jake Hiebert (R21-046, R23-056, R26-037); Damian Penner (R22-038, R24-054, R25-060)
notes: 2018 and 2019 counts were not discussed at recorded meetings (2018 accepted by consensus Jan 2, 2018 per minutes; no 2019-2020 transcript discussion besides Feb 18, 2020).

title: Old Tom Road paved as a boundary road; councillors later call it an "unofficial bypass" of PTH 12
summary: The 2016 financial plan put $1M toward asphalting Old Tom Road on the city's east edge as part of its boundary (periphery) roads program, and council approved the full tender in May 2016 despite a roughly $200,000 overrun. In January 2017 a councillor, very likely Jac Siemens (medium-confidence attribution), described the newly improved Industrial Road and Old Tom Road as 'unofficial bypasses' around Steinbach that would change turning traffic at Park Road and PTH 12.
status_detail: Old Tom Road was paved in 2016. Over the following years residents and councillors described Old Tom, Park Road and Hespeler as a de facto perimeter route around Main Street and PTH 12 (see 2019-clearspring-perimeter-road and 2022-old-tom-loewen-bypass-route).
figures: Budget $1M; low tender $1,058,417 (Bituminex), about $200,000 over budget with engineering (transcript 2016-04-05 part 2, 0:23:44; figures carried from the traffic-congestion research).
public: A Clearspring Green resident wrote about speeding on Old Tom Road after paving (May 2016).
notes: Old Tom Road is a city boundary road, not a highway; included because it became the de facto east-side bypass route.

title: Park Road West: from gravel detour (2016) to a paved second route north (2023)
summary: In June 2016 a Councillor Penner noted heavy detour traffic on gravel Park Road West during PTH 12 construction and asked whether it would be surfaced as a peripheral road; the city manager said road upgrades are developer-driven and the mayor said the city's own share would be considered. Councillor Siemens later read the traffic counts as showing drivers using Industrial Road and Park Road 'as a sort of bypass' of the Loewen Blvd/PTH 12 intersection (2020). In March 2023 council paid from reserves to extend the paving to Industrial Road, and members described it as 'a great bypass' and 'another way to go north' during the Loewen rebuild.
status_detail: Park Road West was paved in stages with developer work; the city-funded extension to Industrial Road ($1,970,097, R23-057) was expected to open after Oct 13, 2023. Councillor Siemens said in 2023 that Acres Drive had also more than doubled its traffic when Park Road was closed.
figures: Extension contract $1,970,097 plus taxes, low of 5 bids (minutes R23-057); planned 4-lane profile where land fronting it develops (2016-06-07, 0:14:51).
reasons: development-first: road upgrades are developer-driven (2016) (Troy Warkentin)
notes: 2016 speaker 'Councillor Penner' could be Susan or Cari Penner.

title: McKenzie Ave, a truck route between PTH 12 and the Barkman plant, rebuilt in concrete for heavy trucks
summary: In late 2017 council approved a local improvement to rebuild McKenzie Avenue between Lilac Bay and Brandt Street (PTH 12); councillors said it would be concrete because of heavy truck traffic from Barkman Concrete. The tender went to Maple Leaf Construction in March 2018.
status_detail: Tender awarded (R18-060) and road rebuilt in 2018; McKenzie Ave remains a designated truck route.
figures: Project estimate $810,000 including up to $500,000 borrowing (city manager, 2017-12-19, 0:09:49); tender $514,410 plus taxes (minutes R18-060).
notes: Local industrial truck traffic, not through traffic; included as part of the city's truck-route network.

title: 2018 provincial highway access plan mentions a perimeter/bypass; province calls it 'hypothetical' and the city does not adopt the plan
summary: A Highway Access Management and Transportation Plan for PTH 12 and PTH 52 was prepared and funded jointly by the City, the RM of Hanover and Manitoba Infrastructure and completed in 2018. Per SteinbachOnline (Mar 20, 2018, as cited in the existing report), it mentioned a perimeter highway or bypass, which a provincial official called 'just a hypothetical concept' with nothing planned 'anytime soon'. At the July 17, 2018 hearing on the new Official Community Plan (By-law 2099), the province's planning branch asked the city to reference the access plan and to plan internal roads for land along PTH 52; the city planner replied that the city would not adopt the access plan until Manitoba Infrastructure formally adopted it, and that a city transportation plan was wanted 'within the future' but not immediately. No council member raised the perimeter idea at a meeting.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2099 passed third reading Oct 16, 2018 (R18-242). The access plan was not published; council next cited it in December 2024 (see 2024-hanover-pth12-north-objection). No bypass study followed.
reasons: waiting-on-province: city would not adopt the access plan until Manitoba Infrastructure did (Lacey Gaudet (City Planner)); study-first: a transportation plan is wanted in future, not now (Lacey Gaudet (City Planner))
public: The province's Community and Regional Planning branch (a provincial planner presenting at the hearing) asked that the OCP mention the access management plan and plan internal roads for development next to PTH 52.
notes: The 'hypothetical concept' quote is from SteinbachOnline (Mar 20, 2018) as cited in answers/main-street-bypass; not re-checked here. No 2018-07-17 minutes PDF was available; OCP readings are from the motions CSV.

title: Loewen Blvd/PTH 12 intersection rebuilt with the province instead of moving traffic off the highway
summary: Loewen Blvd at PTH 12 was the worst intersection in the yearly counts. Council secured corner land in 2018 (the corner was 'a trucking route', said Councillor Fehr), passed a $8.275M local improvement plan in 2021-22 with provincial funding for the surface works, and awarded construction in 2024. A neighbouring property owner's son (K.P.) told council that drivers were cutting through Maplewood, Old Tom Road and his yard to avoid the intersection. Councillor Damian Penner said the new design would 'alleviate some of the arterial roads and put it on our main road', and Mayor Funk said it would move more traffic more efficiently.
status_detail: By-law 2187 (LIP 2022-02) passed (R21-250/251, R22-067); construction awarded to Maple Leaf Construction for $9,981,284 (R24-107). The intersection reopened Nov 24, 2025 (about $11.2M, city about $6.1M, per the existing report).
figures: 2021 estimate $8.275M: $3.5M borrowing, $4.545M grants and other funding, $230,000 reserves (city manager, 2021-12-07, 0:19:21); construction tender $9,981,284 (minutes R24-107).
public: K.P., speaking for the family that owns the corner property, said westbound drivers queue on Loewen and cut through side streets and his yard, noted Loewen east of PTH 12 is not a truck route, and asked for three westbound lanes and a median opening.
mover: Jac Siemens (R21-250, R24-107); Michael Zwaagstra (R21-251, R22-067)
seconder: Damian Penner (R21-250); Bill Hiebert (R21-251); Susan Penner (R22-067); Michael Zwaagstra (R24-107)
notes: Intersection detail is covered in the traffic-congestion report; here only as the alternative to a bypass.

title: How Main Street became a rebuilt highway through downtown, with side streets upgraded as alternate truck routes (history told by Councillor Siemens)
summary: In his opening remarks on July 17, 2018, Councillor Siemens recounted Main Street's reconstruction: in the 1980s Hespeler, Loewen and McKenzie were upgraded 'to handle the truck traffic' and Elmdale connected 'to provide alternate traffic routes to the main street', and from 1989 to the mid-1990s the city, with Manitoba Highways' approval and money for the highway portion, rebuilt Main Street (PTH 52) as a four-lane highway through downtown. The history shows the long-standing approach: keep the provincial highway through the centre and build city streets as relief routes.
notes: Transcript starts mid-sentence at 0:00:00; dates of the works are as Siemens told them, not checked against other records.

title: Residents: Park Road, Old Tom and Hespeler 'became a perimeter road around Steinbach'
summary: A July 2019 delegation of Clearspring Greens residents asked for a pathway because paving Old Tom Road had turned Park Road, Old Tom and Hespeler into a busy, fast route around the city. One resident said Highway 12 was basically the only north-south road and that the edge roads had become a perimeter road. The mayor said the 2019 budget did not allow work and a plan was coming.
status_detail: Council added streetlights at Old Tom/Park Rd (R19-033) and later a pathway (cost split capped at $1,610 per lot, R21-012), per the traffic-congestion research; nothing was done about the volume of traffic using the edge roads as a bypass.
reasons: cost: the 2019 budget did not allow anything in that area (Earl Funk)
public: Resident D. (Mooney Ave) and other Clearspring Greens residents said children could not safely walk or bike on Old Tom/Park Road because of fast through traffic.
mover: Jake Hiebert (R19-033); Damian Penner (R20-005); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-012)
seconder: Bill Hiebert (R19-033); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-005); Damian Penner (R20-012)
vote: R20-005 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert) and R20-012 6-1 (against: Siemens), both on who pays for the pathway
notes: The divided votes were about cost-sharing for a pathway, not about traffic routing; they are listed in the traffic-congestion data.

title: Regional highway lobbying: twin PTH 59, four-lane PTH 52 east and west, PTH 12 overlay; no bypass on the list
summary: Council supported St. Pierre-Jolys' request to twin PTH 59 to PTH 52 (2019) and in 2024 joined the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee to lobby the province together. Councillor Siemens, appointed as delegate, listed his highway priorities: a PTH 12 overlay north of McKenzie, four-laning PTH 59, a four-lane PTH 52 to PTH 59, and a four-lane PTH 52 between Steinbach and La Broquerie. He later reported raising PTH 12, 52 and 59 with regional highway staff and Highways Minister Lisa Naylor (Oct 22, 2025). None of the asks was a bypass or truck route around Steinbach.
status_detail: Memberships and appointment approved (R24-170, R24-176, R25-087); results of the ministerial meeting were not reported at a recorded council meeting. The province's 2026 PTH 12 resurfacing north of Park Road adds no lanes (existing report).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R19-268, R24-176); Jac Siemens (R24-170, R25-087)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R19-268, R24-176); Michael Zwaagstra (R24-170); Damian Penner (R25-087)
notes: No transcript of Dec 17, 2019; PTH 59 support from minutes R19-268.

title: Bush Farm Road and other edge roads: upgraded only as development fronts them
summary: At a March 2020 hearing on the next Parkhill phase, Bush Farm Road resident G.H. objected that the gravel road carries heavy traffic in the southwest and asked when it would be improved. The city manager said developers build the roads fronting their land, so no upgrade was required; Mayor Funk said council needed a plan for how its edge roads would handle growth. In 2021 council widened the Bush Farm Road right-of-way for utilities and drainage (By-law 2181).
status_detail: Right-of-way widened (By-law 2181: R21-167, R21-168, R21-184). No plan for the edge roads as a ring around the city came to a public meeting; the 2025 development plan maps no ring road (existing report).
reasons: development-first: roads are built by the developer of fronting land (Troy Warkentin)
public: G.H. (Bush Farm Road) objected that waiting for full development to pave the road 'seems a little bit regressive'.
mover: Susan Penner, Jake Hiebert (2020); Michael Zwaagstra, Jake Hiebert, Michael Zwaagstra (2021)
seconder: Damian Penner, Jac Siemens (2020); Jac Siemens, Bill Hiebert, Jake Hiebert (2021)
notes: Whether a study session took up Bush Farm Road is unknown (not recorded).

title: Truck rules: through trucks kept on PTH 12 and 52; engine-brake signs requested, weight enforcement and fines added
summary: Steinbach's designated truck routes are PTH 12 (Brandt St), PTH 52 (Main St) and McKenzie Ave (city truck-route page, 2026), so through trucks are routed along Main Street and Brandt Street. Staff told council in 2021 that trucks keep to designated routes except to reach permitted work sites. In 2022 council asked Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure for 'no engine brake' signs on all four highway entrances after residents south of the city complained; in 2023 it joined the province's Community Safety Officer program to weigh heavy vehicles; in 2025 Traffic By-law 2254 banned engine retarder brakes and raised fines for parked heavy vehicles.
status_detail: R22-177 (signs) sent; no reply or installation reported. R23-036 (weight enforcement) agreed. By-law 2254 adopted (R25-015, R25-016). No review of truck routes or count of trucks was made.
figures: Engine retarder brake fine $100 ($50 early payment); heavy vehicle parked over 2 hours $500 ($250) (Nov 5, 2024 package, per traffic-congestion research).
reasons: provincial-highway: signs on provincial highways need the province and a council resolution (Adam Thiessen)
public: Residents south of the city complained of engine-brake noise (via Councillor Bill Hiebert).
mover: Bill Hiebert (R22-177); Michael Zwaagstra (R23-036); Jac Siemens (R25-015); Jake Hiebert (R25-016)
seconder: Jac Siemens (R22-177, R23-036); Bill Hiebert (R25-015); Damian Penner (R25-016)
notes: Truck-route list from the current City of Steinbach truck-route page (Acres Dr and Industrial Rd, listed in an earlier version of this report, are not on it); the 2021-09-07 staff answer is not quoted because its speaker label also carries a councillor.

title: Residents say Old Tom and Loewen are 'a city bypass and speedway'; council approves new homes without a traffic study
summary: At the Sept 6, 2022 hearing for a 95-parcel neighbourhood at Old Tom Road and Loewen Blvd, residents asked for a traffic study and plans for the Loewen intersections; R.F. said the roads are 'being used as a city bypass and speedway'. Councillor Siemens agreed the city's traffic is 'horrendous' and that paving Old Tom had made it 'a way to bypass Highway 12 and our main street', said traffic flow is discussed at long-term planning sessions, but there was 'not a definitive plan'. Mayor Funk said roads follow development. Council approved unanimously.
status_detail: No traffic study was required and no plan for Old Tom/Loewen was adopted; a 3-way stop at Loewen and Hespeler was defeated in 2024 and a roundabout not budgeted (existing reports).
reasons: development-first: let development happen, then work on the road system (Earl Funk); study-first: handled in long-term planning sessions; no definitive plan (Jac Siemens)
public: R.F. (Loewen Blvd) asked for a traffic impact study and active-transportation plan first; D.E. asked for a count outside construction; J.C. asked about the Loewen intersections.

title: Complaints about the time to drive through Steinbach answered with signal timing, not a new route
summary: In January 2023 Councillor Siemens relayed complaints about 'the amount of time it takes to drive through Steinbach' on PTH 12 and asked that the province review signal timing and turn lanes; Councillor Zwaagstra said a trip from the south end to Clearspring Mall had taken almost 25 minutes. Council's consensus was for staff to meet Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure. The same complaint, 'how long it takes to get out of town', returned with the 2024 and 2025 studies, which recommended retiming PTH 12 signals; Siemens opposed possible signals at Lund Rd ('3 sets of traffic lights in one block').
status_detail: Staff met MTI (city manager's report, May 2, 2023 minutes); MTI was reviewing PTH 12 timing in March 2025 per staff; members were still calling the lights unsynchronized in February 2026.
figures: Almost 25 minutes from the Meadows to Clearspring Mall at a December 2022 peak (Zwaagstra, 2023-01-03, 0:22:57).
reasons: provincial-highway: MTI manages all traffic signals in Steinbach (Troy Warkentin)

title: Truck yard denied; Councillor Siemens worries about more trucks on Main Street, which 'go south on 12' to the border
summary: Council unanimously denied a conditional use for a trucking company's yard at 45 Tower Avenue after neighbours objected. Councillor Susan Penner asked whether trucks would stay on PTH 12 and 52; the city manager said they would have to use PTH 52, a designated truck route. Councillor Siemens said his first concern was additional truck traffic on Main Street, adding that trucks generally go south on PTH 12 to the border.
status_detail: Conditional use denied (R24-009); status refers to the applicant's request.
figures: Applicant had 19 trucks; the 4-acre yard could hold about 60 (minutes Jan 16, 2024, per traffic-congestion research).
public: Neighbours objected to noise, lights, dust, safety and traffic; one said it would add traffic on Main Street.

title: City objects to RM of Hanover rezoning on PTH 12 North that ignored the 2018 highway access plan
summary: In December 2024 council filed an objection to an RM of Hanover rezoning of land just north of the city on PTH 12 North, where businesses had already been built. The city manager said the development did not appear to follow the 2018 Highway Access Management and Transportation Plan for PTH 12 and 52, prepared jointly by the City, Hanover and the province, nor Hanover's own development plan and the annexation agreement. Councillors Susan Penner and Zwaagstra said land next to the city must stay compatible with its growth and that highway upgrades should have been triggered.
status_detail: Objection filed (R24-246) ahead of Hanover's Jan 8, 2025 hearing; the outcome was not reported at a recorded council meeting.
notes: Zwaagstra, repeating the city manager, called it a 2013 plan in his turn; the city manager said 2018.

title: New development plan protects land for future highway works in general terms but maps no bypass or ring road
summary: Council adopted a new Official Community Plan (By-law 2244) in 2025. Per the existing report, it says land 'shall be protected for … any future highway system enhancements, such as interchanges, highway realignments, or new corridors', names only a PTH 52 realignment at Bushfarm and Keating Rds, and treats PTH 12 and 52 as heavy-truck routes to be 'preserved as major highway corridors'. Its maps show no bypass or ring-road corridor. No council member spoke about highway corridors at the recorded readings.
status_detail: Adopted (R25-069, R25-070, R25-184). General corridor protection only; the bypass question is left unsettled in the plan.
mover: Jac Siemens (1st); Jake Hiebert (2nd); Susan Penner (3rd)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (1st); Bill Hiebert (2nd); Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
notes: OCP wording from answers/main-street-bypass (Official Community Plan pp. 13-16 and Reference Map 1); not re-read here.

title: Residents report trucks and cut-through traffic on McKenzie Ave and Friesen Ave; no truck-route review
summary: At 2026 hearings on infill housing, residents described heavy trucks using city streets. On McKenzie Ave (a four-lane truck route), H.K. said many eastbound tractor-trailers turn right toward La Broquerie on PTH 52 East, using the curb lane. On Friesen Ave, P.H. said the street 'has become like a major hub for truck transport' although it is not a truck route, and drivers from Main Street use it as a shortcut. Councillor Zwaagstra said the main traffic on McKenzie is people going through, not residents. Council approved both projects; no truck-route review or truck count was requested. Earlier, a resident had asked (Dec 2025) about delivery trucks on First Street, and staff said traffic studies are required only for impacts on PTH 12 and 52.
status_detail: Rezoning and housing approvals passed; the truck concerns received no response or follow-up at council.
reasons: no-data: traffic impact studies are required only for impacts on PTH 12 and PTH 52 (Dec 2025, per traffic-congestion research) (Troy Warkentin)
public: H.K. (McKenzie Ave, 57 years) and P.H. (Friesen Ave) described trucks and through traffic on residential and collector streets; R.P. (Dec 2025) raised delivery trucks on First Street. These are residents' observations, not measured.
notes: Whether trucks on Friesen or McKenzie are through trucks or local deliveries is not known; no counts exist.

title: 'Traffic comes to Steinbach, it doesn't go through': Councillor Siemens dismisses a bypass as the 2025 traffic study is accepted
summary: Presenting the 2025 WSP study, the city manager said PTH 12 at Main Street carried nearly 3,500 vehicles an hour at peak and that MTI manages all signals; the recommendations were 'not must-haves'. Mayor Funk said many vehicles come in from the west every morning to work. Councillor Siemens said he is always asked why Steinbach isn't building a bypass, but the yearly reports show 'traffic comes to Steinbach, it doesn't go through' so 'a bypass Doesn't make sense'; he also noted counts are taken in autumn during construction. Nobody responded, and council accepted the report. This is the only time a member of council spoke directly to a highway bypass on the record from 2015 to 2026.
status_detail: Report accepted (R26-037, unanimous); no motion, budget item or request about a bypass, perimeter road, origin-destination survey or truck count followed by Nov 2026.
figures: Busiest intersection PTH 12/PTH 52 (Main St) nearly 3,500 vehicles per hour at peak (city manager, 0:14:17); 20 intersections counted (0:14:17).
reasons: traffic-comes-to-steinbach: the yearly studies show traffic comes to Steinbach rather than through it (Jac Siemens); provincial-highway: MTI is the authority over signals on the highways (Troy Warkentin)
notes: The study counts turning movements, not trips; it cannot directly show how much traffic passes through (see existing report).
